notes: 'Ours' = the unified trial-level memory model (v10 checkpoint of 2026-09-07 unless stated); one model for all datasets, no dataset-specific parameters.
Published-model numbers were verified at source (summary/note-0906-sota-survey.md); 'not surveyed' means no verified number.
Figures are clipped from the original open-access papers or author manuscripts for academic summary; each carries its source and licence.

figure.title: Item memorability has no influence on value-based decisions
figure.authors: Xinyue Li, Wilma A. Bainbridge, Akram Bakkour
figure.caption_short: Continuous recognition memorability task: participants view a stream of single-object photographs (1 s each, separated by a fixation cross) and press the 'r' key when an image repeats after a delay of more than 120 s.
figure.notes: FALLBACK FIGURE - NOT from the original THINGS-memorability paper. The original dataset paper (Kramer, Hebart, Baker & Bainbridge, 'The features underlying the memorability of objects', Science Advances 9:eadd2981, 2023, https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.add2981, CC BY-NC 4.0, saved as site/papers/things_mem.pdf) contains NO task-paradigm figure: its four main figures (Figs. 1-4) and its seven supplementary figures (figs. S1-S7) are all analysis plots, and the bioRxiv preprint (10.1101/2022.04.29.490104, saved as site/papers/tm_pre.pdf) has the same four figures. The project OSF repository (https://osf.io/5a7z6) contains only data tables, no task diagram. The figure used here is Figure 1A of Li, Bainbridge & Bakkour (2022), a study from the same senior lab (W. A. Bainbridge) that uses the same online continuous-recognition repeat-detection paradigm with single-object photographs and the same 'r' key response; PDF saved as site/papers/things_mem_paradigm_fallback.pdf. Differences from the actual THINGS experiment as described in the Science Advances Methods: THINGS used 500 ms image presentation with an 800 ms interstimulus interval, a minimum 60 s (not 120 s) delay before a target repeat, vigilance repeats 1-5 images apart, and 187 THINGS object images per participant (N = 13,946 AMT participants). Crop is panel A only; panel B (a value-based choice task, irrelevant here) and the caption are excluded. Rendered at 220 dpi.

datasets.published_metric: LDI = p(similar|lure) − p(similar|foil); REC = p(old|target) − p(old|foil); lure-bin gradient

sota.note: all trial-level models are stimulus-blind (inputs = condition labels)

figure.authors: Michael J. Kahana, Lynn J. Lohnas, M. Karl Healey, Ada Aka, Adam W. Broitman, Patrick Crutchley, Elizabeth Crutchley, Kylie H. Alm, Brandon S. Katerman, Nicole E. Miller, Joel R. Kuhn, Yuxuan Li, Nicole M. Long, Jonathan Miller, Madison D. Paron, Jesse K. Pazdera, Isaac Pedisich, Joseph H. Rudoler, Christoph T. Weidemann
figure.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition 50(9):1421-1443
figure.caption_short: The end-of-session recognition path in PEERS: after studying 16 lists of 16 words and doing immediate free recall, subjects take an item-recognition test with confidence judgements (and, in half the sessions, a 5-minute final free-recall test first).
figure.license: author manuscript, PMC (NIHMS-2084225); published version copyright American Psychological Association - figure reproduced under fair use for academic summary
figure.notes: This is the SAME Figure 1 as peers_recall.png, not a separate figure. The paper contains no dedicated panel or screenshot of the recognition response screen or of the confidence scale, so per instructions this crop is the sub-region of Figure 1 (the Experiments 1 and 3 row) that contains the 'Item Recognition with Conf. Judgments' branch; use peers_recall.png if a single shared figure is preferred. Recognition procedure per the paper's Methods ('Measuring Recognition'): responses were vocal - subjects said 'pess' or 'po' instead of 'yes'/'no' so that the stop consonant gave precise response timing - and confidence ratings were collected after the old/new decision; subjects were incentivised for speed on the yes/no response and for accuracy via the confidence judgement. The paper does not state the number of confidence levels in this figure or its caption. Cropped from a 220-dpi render of p. 32.

figure.title: Comparing memory capacity across stimuli requires maximally dissimilar foils: Using deep convolutional neural networks to understand visual working memory capacity for real-world objects
figure.authors: Timothy F. Brady, Viola S. Störmer
figure.caption_short: Method of Experiment 2: participants saw six real-world objects for 2000 ms, held them over a 700 ms delay, and then made a two-alternative forced choice at a cued location between the studied object and a foil.
figure.license: publisher copyright (© The Psychonomic Society, Inc. 2023; Springer Nature holds exclusive rights under a publishing agreement) — author self-archived PDF of the published version from the Brady lab website; used under fair use for academic summary
figure.notes: Cropped from page 8 (journal page 602) of the published typeset PDF at 440 dpi; caption text excluded. Fig. 4 shows the full trial: 6-object memory array (2000 ms, spatial placeholders visible throughout) -> 700 ms delay -> 2-AFC test at one cued location with the studied object and one foil. The foil-similarity manipulation is described in the caption rather than drawn as separate panels: foils were maximally distinct cross-category, minimally distinct cross-category, or randomly chosen from a different category (60 trials each, 180 total, N = 50 MTurk participants). The example pairs for the similarity conditions are shown separately in Fig. 2, and the CNN foil-selection method in Fig. 1. Fig. 6 (page 10) is the analogous method figure for Experiment 3, which contrasts objects with colors. Not open access: Crossref registers only a Springer Nature text-and-data-mining license (no CC license), and no PMC record was found. The OSF node https://osf.io/axyqs/ is a public project holding materials, data and analysis code — the OSF preprints API returns 404 for that identifier, so it is not a preprint. The author self-archived copy at bradylab.ucsd.edu was therefore used.

figure.notes: Cropped from page 3 (journal page 126) of the published APA typeset PDF at 440 dpi; caption text excluded. Figure 2 is the paper's schematic of the delayed-estimation paradigm (memory array -> delay -> continuous report on a color wheel). The delayed-estimation benchmark analysed in this paper pools 10 previously published experiments (Table 1, same page): E1 Wilken & Ma 2004 (color wheel, Caltech); E2 Zhang & Luck 2008 (color wheel, UC Davis); E3 Bays et al. 2009 (color wheel, UCL); E4 Anderson et al. 2011 (orientation 360deg, U Oregon); E5 Anderson & Awh 2012 (orientation 180deg, U Oregon); E6 Anderson & Awh 2012 (orientation 360deg, U Oregon); E7-E9 Van den Berg et al. 2012 (color scrolling, color wheel, orientation 180deg; Baylor); E10 Rademaker et al. 2012 (orientation 180deg, Vanderbilt). Combined: 164 subjects, 131,452 trials. Figure 2 illustrates the color-wheel version; orientation experiments used an analogous continuous report. Data and code: https://github.com/WeiJiMaLab/delayed_estimation_benchmark. The PMC author-manuscript version is PMC4159389 (its PDF is behind a proof-of-work challenge; the Ma lab copy was used instead — note the task brief cited PMC3949221, but Unpaywall/PMC resolve DOI 10.1037/a0035234 to PMC4159389).
